paratext: explicit: f. 142v Τὸ ἀργύριον καὶ τὸ χρυσίον ἐμόν ἐστιν· ὁ οὐρανὸς θρόνος ἐμὸς· ἡ γῆ ὑποπόδιον τῶν ποδῶν μου

paratext: explicit: f. 180v μετὰ πολλῆς τῆς περιουσίας τοὺς ἀγαθόν τι ποιεῖν ἢ λέγειν προαιρουμένους. νικᾶν ἐσπούδακεν ταῖς ἀντιδόσεσι καὶ ταῖς ἀμοιβαῖς
paratext: rubric(s): f. 146v Τοῦ αὐτοῦ ἀπὸ ἐξορίας ἀπολογία πρὸς τοὺς σκανδαλισθέντας ἐπὶ ταῖς παρανομίαις ταῖς γινομέναις καὶ τῆ τοῦ λαοῦ. καὶ πολλῶν ἱερέων διώξει καὶ διασπορα

paratext: explicit: f. 191r οὕτω γὰρ καὶ τὸν δεσπότην ἡμῖν. κὰν μυρία ὦμεν ἡμαρτηκότες καταλλάξομεν· καὶ τῶν μελλόντων ἐπιτύχωμεν ἀγαθῶν· ὧν γένοιτο πάντας ἡμᾶς ἐπιτυχεῖν· χάριτι καὶ φιλανθρωπία τοῦ Κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ· μεθ' οὕτω Πατρὶ ἅμα τῶ ἅγίω Πνεύματι· δόξα κράτος τιμῆ. νῦν καὶ ἀεὶ καὶ εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων ἀμήν
paratext: rubric(s): f. 180v Τοῦ αὐτοῦ εἰς το διαχρόνου εἰπεῖν· καὶ εἰς τὴν παραβολὴν τοῦ τα μύρια τάλαντα ὀφείλοντος· καὶ τὰ εκατὸν δινάρια ἀπαιτοῦντος· καὶ ὅτι παντὸς ἁμαρτήματος τὸ μνησικακεῖν χεῖρον

paratext: incipit: f. 191r Ὅτε τὸν ἐν Ἱεροσολύμοις ναὸν πολλῶν ἐτῶν χαμαὶ κείμενον ἀπὸ τῆς μακρᾶς ἐπανελθόντες αἰχμαλωσίας
paratext: explicit: f. 242v καὶ πάντων ἀπολαύσονται τῶν ἀγαθῶν. ὑμῖν δὲ περίεστε τὸ μυρίαν κόλασιν ἑαυτοῖς συναγαγεῖν· καὶ τότε ἐπαινέσαι τὰ παρ’ ἡμῶν εἰρημένα. ὅτε τῶν ἐπαίνων ὑμῖν ὤφελος οὐδέν
paratext: rubric(s): f. 191r Τοῦ αὐτοῦ πρὸς τοὺς πολεμοῦντας τοῖς ἐπὶ τὸ μονάζειν ἄγουσιν

paratext: explicit: f. 267r τούτου οὐ κάπτεται καύσων· ὑπὸ τούτω τῶ φυτῶ. εὐφραίνου καὶ χόρευε μεταγγέλων. δοξάζων τὸν Πατέρα καὶ τὸν Υἱὸν καὶ τὸ ἅγιον Πνεῦμα· νῦν καὶ ἀεὶ καὶ εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων ἀμήν

work: title: In illud: Ignem veni mittere in terram
paratext: incipit: f. 274v Αἱ τῶν νηπίων φιλότεκνοι μητέρες. μέχρις δὰν προς μείζονα ἡλικίαν καὶ δυνατωτέραν οἱ νήπιοι αὐξηθῶσιν
paratext: explicit: f. 277v πρὸς ἀγάπην Θεοῦ. καὶ ἀλλήλων τὰς λαμπάδας ἀνάψη ἐν Χριστῶ Ἰησοῦ τῶ κυρίω ἡμῶν· ὧ ἡ δόξα εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰωνων ἀμήν

work: title: In illud: Sufficit tibi gratia mea
paratext: incipit: f. 278v Ὅτε τὸν παναρμῶνιον τουτονεὶ κόσμον ἐξ αρχῆς ἔπλαττεν ὁ Θεὸς. θαύματα ἐπι θαύμασιν εἰργάσατο

work: title: In epistulam I ad Thessalonicenses homilia 8
paratext: incipit: f. 286r Οἱ προφήται μὲν τὸ ἀξιόπιστον τῶν λεγομένων δεῖξαι βουλόμενοι. πρὸ τῶν ἄλλων ἁπάντων. τοῦτο λέγουσιν
paratext: explicit: f. 290v μήτε ἐπι καρδίαν ἀνθρώπου ἀνέβη· ὧν γένοιτο πάντας ἡμᾶς ἐπιτυχεῖν χάριτι καὶ φιλανθρωπία τοῦ Κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ· μεθοῦ τῶ Πατρὶ. ἅμα τῶ ἁγίω Πνεύματι. δόξα κράτος τιμὴ· νῦν καὶ ἀεὶ καὶ εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων ἀμήν
paratext: rubric(s): f. 286r Τοῦ αὐτοῦ εἰς τὸ τοῦτο γὰρ παρ’ ὑμῖν λέγωμεν ἐν λόγω Κυρίου· ὅτι ἡμεῖς οἱ ζῶντες οἱ περιλειπόμενοι εἰς τὴν παρουσίαν τοῦ Κυρίου οὐ μὴ φθάσωμεν τοὺς κυμηθέντας· ὅτι αὐτὸς ὁ Κύριος ἐν κελεύματι· ἐν φωνῆ ἀρχαγγέλου· ἐν σάλπιγγι Θεοῦ καταβήσεται ἀπ’ οὐρανοῦ. καὶ οἱ νεκροὶ ἐν Χριστῶ ἀναστήσονται πρῶτοι· ἔπιτα ἡμεῖς οἱ ζῶντες οἱ περιλειπόμενοι. ἅμα σὺν αὐτοῖς ἁρπαγησόμεθα· ἐν νεφέλαις· εἰς ἀπάντησιν τοῦ Κυρίου εἰς ἀέρα. καὶ οὕτω πάντοτε σὺν Κυρίω ἐσώμεθα

work: title: In illud: Si qua in Christo nova creatura
paratext: incipit: f. 290v Πολλὴ μὲν γηπόνω προθυμία καταβάλλειν τὰ σπέρματα. ἐπειδὰν τὴν ἄρουραν ἐκκεκαθαρμένην ἴδη
paratext: explicit: f. 298r αὐτὴν εὐλάβειαν ὡς ὁ πτωχὸς καὶ ἐγώ· ὥστε εἴ τις ἐν Χριστῶ καινὴ κτησις· ὑπὲρ δὲ τούτων ἁπάντων εὐχαριστήσωμεν τῶ Θεῶ. ὅτι αὐτῶ ἡ δόξα εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας ἀμήν
paratext: rubric(s): f. 290v Τοῦ αὐτοῦ εἰς τὸ εἴ τις ἐν Χριστῶ καινὴ κτίσης· τὰ ἀρχαια παρῆλθον. ἰδοὺ γέγονε τὰ πάντα καινά
bibliography: note(s): Attributed to Chrysostom.; PG 64, 25-34; CPG 4701; Aldama 427; TLG 2062.359

work: title: In sanctum Paulum Apostolum (defective at the beginning)

work: title: In Illud: Hic est filius meus dilectus
paratext: incipit: f. 303v Ὁ μὲν γιλόστοργος οὗτος πατὴρ διὰ τῆν περὶ ἡμᾶς στοργῆν ἔπεμψεν μοι τοῦ λόγου τὸ σύνθεμα
paratext: explicit: f. 307v αὐτὸς συναθρύσειεν εἰς τὰς ἑαυτοῦ μάνδρας τὰ πλανώμενα πρόβατα .ἵνα γένηται μία ποίμνη εἰς ποιμὴν· ἐν Χριστῶ Ἰησοῦ τῶ Κυρίω ἡμῶν. ὧ ἡ δόξα εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων ἀμήν
paratext: rubric(s): f. 303v Τοῦ αὐτοῦ εἰς τὸ οὗτός ἔστιν ὁ υἱός μου ὁ ἀγαπητὸς ἐν ῶ ηὐδοίκησα

work: title: De patientia et de consummatione huius saeculi
paratext: incipit: f. 307v Λαμπρὸς ὁ βίος τῶν δικαίων· πῶς δὲ λαμπρύνεται. ἀλλ’ ἢ διὰ τῆς ὑπομονῆς· ταύτην ἀγάπησον ὦ ἀδελφὲ
paratext: explicit: f. 313v ἐνώπιον τοῦ δικαίου κριτοῦ. τοῦ ἀποδόντος ἑκάστω κατὰ τὰ ἔργα αὐτοῦ· ὧ πρέπει δόξα σὺν τῷ παντοκράτορι Πατρὶ καὶ τῶ ἁγίω Πνεύματι· νῦν καὶ ἀεὶ καὶ εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων ἀμήν
paratext: rubric(s): f. 307v Τοῦ αὐτοῦ λόγος περὶ ὑπομονῆς· καὶ περὶ συντελείας τοῦ αἰῶνος τούτου· καὶ δευτέρας τοῦ Κυρίου παρουσίας· ἀδιαδόχου τε τῶν δικαίων βασιλείας· καὶ ἀτελευτήτου τῶν ἁμαρτωλῶν κολάσεως. ὑπόθεσίς τε ἐξομολογήσεως· καὶ πρὸς τὴν τῶν θείων γραφῶν μελέτην προτροπὴ. τίνες τὲ αἱ μεθοδίαι τοῦ ἐχθροῦ. καὶ τί τὸ τῆς ἡσυχίας ὀφέλημον
bibliography: note(s): Attributed to Chrysostom.; PG 63, 937-942; CPG 4693; Aldama 238; TLG 2062.351

work: title: In evangelii dictum et de virginitate (defective at the end)
paratext: incipit: f. 313v Οὐδὲν ὁ θεῖος λόγος ἀσκόπως. οὐδὲ ξένον τῆς ἡμετέρας σωτηρίας παρέδωκεν αἴνιγμα
paratext: explicit: f. 316r ἄρα γὰρ ταύτην ἡδονὴν ἔστιν ἐπει ἡ ἀπόλαυσιν βίου· ἆρα τοῦτο τρυφὴ; τοῦτο πλάτος; τις αὕτη τῆς μανίας ἡ συγκατάθεσις
paratext: rubric(s): f. 313v Τοῦ αὐτοῦ εἰς τὸ τοῦ εὐαγγελίου ῥητὸν. καὶ περὶ παρθενείας. καὶ παραινετικὸς εἰς τὰς ἐκπεσούσας
bibliography: note(s): Attributed to Chrysostom.; PG 64, 37-40 line 19; CPG 4702; Aldama 358; TLG 2062.360

paratext: incipit: f. 316r Τί δὲ καὶ ὑμῖν ἄθλιοι καὶ ταλαίπωροι κακῶν ἡδονῶν ὁδηγοί· πῶς βούλεσθαι ἐκφυγεῖν χεῖρας Θεοῦ ζῶντος
paratext: explicit: f. 319r ὁ Πατὴρ τῶν οἰκτιρμῶν καὶ Θεὸς πάσης παρακλήσεως· χάριτι καὶ οἰκτιρμοῖς καὶ φιλανθρωπία τοῦ Κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ μεθ’ οὗ πρέπει δόξα τιμὴ καὶ προσκύνησις. σὺν τῶ παναγίω καὶ ἀγαθῶ καὶ ζωοποιῶ Πνεύματι· νῦν καὶ ἀεὶ καὶ εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων ἀμήν
paratext: rubric(s): f. 316r Ταλανισμὸς πρὸς τοὺς φθείροντας τὰς τοῦ Χριστοῦ παρθένους

work: title: Commentarium in evangelium Matthaei libri X-XVII
paratext: incipit: f. 1r Τότε ἀφεὶς τοὺς ὄχλους, ἦλθεν εἰς τὴν οἰκίαν αὐτοῦ· καὶ προσῆλθον οἱ μαθηταὶ αὐτοῦ λέγοντες· φράσον ἡμῖν τὴν παραβολὴν τῶν ζιζανίων τοῦ ἀγροῦ: Ὅτε μὲν μετὰ τῶν ὄχλων ἐστὶν ὁ Ἰησοῦς, οὐκ ἔστιν αὐτοῦ ἐν τῆ οἰκία
paratext: explicit: f. 214r τὴν διδαχὴν ἀποδεχόμενοι τοῦ σωτῆρος σοφωτάτην καὶ δυναμένην τοὺς δυσπίστως ἔχοντας, ἐπιστρέψαι πρὸς αὐτόν
paratext: rubric(s): f. 1r Ὠριγένους ἐκ τῶν εἰς τὸ κατὰ Ματθαῖον ἐξηγητικων τόμος ιαʹ

paratext: incipit: f. 215r Τὰ διὰ τὸ εἶναι μέγιστα καὶ ὑπὲρ ἄνθρωπον τυγχάνειν. εἰς ὑπερβολήν τὲ ὑπὲρ ἄνω τῆς ἐπικήρου φύσεως ἡμῶν ἀδύνατα τῷ λογικῷ καὶ θνητῷ γένει καταλαβεῖν ἐν πολλῇ
paratext: explicit: f. 252v διαλαβεῖν μεγαλοφυέστερον καὶ ὑψηλότερον καὶ τρανότερον· πλὴν ἐπὶ τοῦ παρόντος μετὰ συγγνώμης τούτοις ἐντεύξεσθε

paratext: incipit: f. 1r Τῆς Χριστοῦ κηρύττουσι

paratext: explicit: f. 21v ὧν γένοιτο πάντας ἡμᾶς ἐπιτυχεῖν· χάριτι καὶ φιλανθρωπία, τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ μεθοῦ τῶι πατρὶ ἡ δόξα ἅμα τῶι ἁγίω πνεύματι νῦν καὶ εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων ἀμήν
paratext: rubric(s): f. 15v Τοῦ αὐτοῦ ὁμιλία ὅτε Σατορνῖνος Αὐρηλιανὸς ἐξωρίσθησαν, καὶ Γαϊνᾶς ἐξῆλθε τῆς πόλεως· καὶ περὶ φιλαργυρίας

paratext: incipit: f. 21v Ἀεὶ μὲν μάλιστα δὲ νῦν εὔκαιρον εἰπεῖν· ματαιότης ματαιοτήτων, καὶ πάντα ματαιότης
paratext: explicit: ff. 35v ἵνα καὶ αὐτοὶ τῶν μελλόντων ἀγαθῶν ἐπιτύχωμεν· χάριτι καὶ φιλανθρωπία τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ ὧ ἡ δόξα εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων ἀμήν
paratext: rubric(s): f. 21v Τοῦ αὐτοῦ ὁμιλία εἰς Εὐτρόπιον εὐνοῦχον πατρίκιον καὶ ὕπατον

paratext: incipit: f. 35v Ἡδὺ μὲν λειμὼν καὶ παράδεισος, πολὺ δὲ ἡδίων γραφῶν ἀνάγνωσις καὶ γνῶσις
paratext: explicit: f. 49r Ὑπὲρ δὴ τούτων ἁπάντων εὐχαριστήσωμεν τῶι Θεῶι ὅτι αὐτῶι ἡ δόξαεἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. Ἀμήν
paratext: rubric(s): f. 35v Τοῦ αὐτοῦ ὁμιλία ὅτε τῆς ἐκκλησίας ἔξω εὑρεθεὶς Εὐτρόπιος ἀπεσπάσθη· καὶ εἰς τὸ παρέστη ἡ βασίλισσα ἐκ δεξιῶν σου ἐν ἱματισμῶ διαχρύσω

paratext: incipit: f. 49r Οἱ σοφώτατοι τῶν ἰατρῶν ἐπὶ δὰν ἴδωσιν ἕλκος σιδήρου δεόμενον ἐπάγουσι
paratext: explicit: f. 72v ἵνα καὶ τὰ παρόντα ἡμῖν πράγματα κατὰ ῥοῦν φέρηται, καὶ τῆς μελλούσης ἐπιτύχωμεν ζωῆς· ἧς γένοιτο πάντας ἡμᾶς ἐπιτυχεῖν χάριτι καὶ φιλανθρωπία τοῦ Κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ, μεθοῦ τῶ Πατρὶ ἅμα τῶι ἁγίω Πνεύματι· δόξα τιμὴ κράτος εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων ἀμήν
paratext: rubric(s): f. 49r Τοῦ ἐν ἁγίοις πατρὸς ἡμῶν Ἰωάννου ἀρχιεπισκόπου Κωνσταντινουπόλεως τοῦ Χρυσοστόμου εἰς ἀποστολικὴν ῥῆσιν τὴν λέγουσαν· ἔχοντες δὲ τὸ αὐτὸ πνεῦμα τῆς πίστεως κατὰ τὸ γεγραμμένον καὶ εἰς τὸ ἐπίστευσα διὸ ἐλάλησα καὶ περὶ ἐλεημοσύνης

paratext: incipit: f. 73r Βούλομαι τῆς συνήθους ἅψασθαι πάλιν διδασκαλίας· καὶ τὴν πνευματικὴν ὑμῖν παραθῆναι τράπεζαν
paratext: explicit: f. 153v παροῦσαν ζωὴν μετὰ εὐθυμίας διενεγκεῖν. καὶ τῆς βασιλείας τῶν οὐρανῶν ἐπιτυχεῖν· ἐν Χριστῶ Ἰησοῦ τῶ κυρίω ἡμῶν ὧ ἡ δόξα καὶ τὸ κράτος· ἅμα τῶ Πατρὶ καὶ τῶ ἁγίω Πνεύματι εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων ἀμήν
paratext: rubric(s): f. 73r Τοῦ ἐν ἁγίοις πατρὸς ἡμῶν Ἰωάννου ἀρχιεπισκόπου Κωνσταντινουπόλεως τοῦ Χρυσοστόμου· ὁμιλία πρὸς τοὺς εἰς τὸ ῥητὸν τοῦ Εὐαγγελίου· εἰσέλθετε διὰ τῆς στενῆς πύλης· ὅτι πλατεῖα ἡ πύλη καὶ εὐρύχωρος ἡ ὁδὸς ἡ ἀπάγουσα εἰς τὴν ἀπώλειαν· καὶ πολλοί εἰσιν οἱ εἰσερχόμενοι δι’ αὐτῆς· καὶ πρὸς τὸ τέλει εἰς τὸν Λάζαρον

work: title: Quales ducendae sint uxores; Encomium ad Maximum
paratext: incipit: f. 165v Ὅτι μὲν ἀπελείφθην ὑμῶν τῆ παρελθούση συνάξει. ἤλγησα· ὅτι δὲ πλουσιωτέρας ἀπελαύσατε τραπέζης. ἥσθην
paratext: explicit: f. 187v καὶ τὸν ἐνταῦθα μετὰ ἀδείας ἁπάσης διανύσαι βίον. καὶ εἰς τὴν τῶν οὐρανῶν βασιλείαν εἰσελθεῖν· ἧς γένοιτο πάντας ἡμᾶς ἐπιτυχεῖν, ἐν Χριστῶ Ἰησοῦ τῶ κυρίω ἡμῶν ὧ ἡ δόξα καὶ τὸ κράτος· νῦν καὶ ἀεὶ καὶ εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων ἀμήν

bibliography: note(s): Full transcription. This short text is added by a 15th-century hand to The Lay Folk's Catechism. It lists the five negative consequences of swearing (oaths) by parts of Christ's body. The idea that such oaths re-enact Christ's torments in the Passion was commonly expressed in late medieval textual and visual culture (e.g. see Melissa Mohr, Holy Sh*t: A Brief History of Swearing (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2013), pp. 112-128).

bibliography: note(s): Describes the creation of an amulet: the charm text is written on parchment in the sufferer's own blood, and invokes the names of the Three Magi. Once the amulet has been written, gold, myrrh and frankincense should be put in and the amulet closed up and hung around the sufferer's neck. The patient should be blessed, and when he rises in the morning he should say three Pater Nosters and three Ave Marias, and every day for a month drink three roots of peony with stale ale. Further instructions describe a cure if the sufferer is a child: that the names of the Magi should be written in the child's blood in a 'masere' (i.e. a drinking bowl) and washed with either ale or milk, and the mixture given to the child to drink.

The eele was sould to cardinal armoniac and if the fisherman had not come to aduertise the master of the castel, that he feared that it was the compagnion of the serpent, the cardinal had ben possoned, for it being ready betwen two dishes to be served in, by the cardina[ls] commandment it was cast to a dog which eatinge it swelled incontinent and died. The serpent was as great as the eel, whom the fishermen took raging in the lake in a net and kiled it.
bibliography: note(s): Full transcription. Four accounts about monstrous creatures as told by eye-witnesses to the author (who is probably also the scribe). According to Timmermann (2015), these accounts are alchemical allegories. The first account tells about a winged dragon from the mountain of Baux, perhaps Les-Baux-de-Provence, that was seen flying over Pugeol, perhaps Pujols, Southwestern France. The second account is about a huge adder at Bederide, probably Bedarrides near Avignon in Southeastern France. The third account is about a three-headed serpent that was killed at a castle at Bayon, perhaps Bayonne in Southwestern France. The fourth and final account tells about a great eel and his serpent compagnon and is partly set in Avignon, Southeastern France, referring to a cardinal Armoniac, perhaps Georges d'Armagnac (b. c. 1501, d. 1585), who was appointed cardinal in 1544.

This collection of medical recipes is largely written in French but also features recipes in Italian, Latin, and English. It contains various references to locations and alchemical and medical practitioners: Nymes [Nîmes, Southeastern France] (f. 2:1r) Puluis domini d'Ampvilij (iam grand canestable de France) [probably referring to Henri de Montmorency (1534-1614)), 3rd Duke of Montmorency, Seigneur of Damville, Governer of Languedoc, who was Constable of France between 1593 and 1614] (f. 2:1v) Verole - Mal de Naples (f. 2:2v) morbum Neapolitanum (ff. 2:5r) Dus Castel. [also abbreviated as Castell.] (ff. 2:18r, 2:18v, 2:19r, 2:21r, 2:22r, 2:22v [2x], 2:24r, 2:24v, 2:26r, 2:27r, 2:27v [crossed out], 2:33r, 2:37v, 2:42r) le cheveux ou Barb. [...] est venu de Aleppo du Levant (f. 2:18r) Mr de la Pierre or Dominus de la Pierre (ff. 2:18r, 2:27v, 2:37r, 2:43v, 2:44r, 2:44v, 2:45r, 2:46r, 2:46v [2x], 2:47r [2x], 2:48v, 2:49v, 2:50r, 2:50v [2x], 2:51r, 2:52r) Mr de Castlemount or Dominus de Castelmont, often abbreviated to Ds Castel. (ff. 2:21r, 2:22r, 2:37r, 2:37v, 2:42r, 2:44r, 2:44v, 2:45r, 2:46r, 2:46v [2x], 2:47r [2x], 2:48v, 2:49v, 2:50r, 2:50v [2x], 2:51r) Mr Renauld (f. 2:21r) Hb (f. 2:25r) Ds Chamb: (f. 2:27r, 2:27v, 2:34r [2x], 2:34v, 2:35r, 2:45r) Pomatum domini Petri (f. 2:36v); Mr Lunelli (f. 2:43r) Mr Sceic (f. 2:43v) Mr Danuge [Daunge] (f. 2:43r) Augustin Maulnoyr [or Mauluoyr de Romorantin de Sologne (f. 2:52r) [the name Maulnoyr or Mauluoyr also occurs on f. 2:58v] Hollerius [most likely referring to Jacques Houllier (b. ?1504, d. 1562), known as Jacobus Hollerius Stampani, Professor of Medicine at the University of Paris] (f. 2:63v) On f. 2:4r is an account about a medicine used at an unidentified monastery: Hoc expe[ri]mento monachus nutriuit totum conventum in [crossed out: Al] A[...] cum quo mirabilia fecit, et quando nimia confectus [...]it aetate vendidit tribus sacerdotibus de suo convent[o] pro decem aureis. Some of the recipes feature titles and words that are written in a cypher. In the usual encryption method, vowels have been replaced for their preceding or successive letters in the alphabet (e.g. opxr ifs fscrpfs - jf xngxfnt [=pour les escroet - le unguent] on f. 2:7r); and Dfs fscrpfis encancarides [=Des escrofit encancarides] on f. 2:8v). In another encryption method, vowels have been replaced with the letter q where the number of horizontal strokes through its descender represents the numerical value of a vowel (e.g. [q2]mpl[q1]str[q2] p[q4][q5]r t[q4][q5]t[q4]s [q5][q4][q2]g[...] vlceros [=emplastre pour toutos voeg[...] ulceros] on f. 2:14r). In a third and more unusual encryption method, both consonants and vowels appear to have been scrambled with their preceding and/or successive letters in the alphabet, and a selection of letters has been replaced with symbols. This cypher, which can be found on f. 2:12r of this manuscript but also occurs in Cambridge, Trinity College, MS O.1.13 (see ff. 84r, 120v, 121r). The recipes are accompanied by a drawing of a flask in brown ink on f. 2:33r; and several alchemical vessels in brown ink on ff. 2:64r-2:64v.

work: title: Collection of medical and alchemical recipes
bibliography: note(s): The collection includes instrucions for treating corrupted wine on f. 3:176r, and a recipe entitled confeccio sanguinis veneris, requiring the blood of a young woman who is a virgin, on f. 3:179r-3:179v. This recipe, as well as the Emplastrum quod vocatur Neyrbon sic fiet on ff. 3:180r-3:180v may have been extracted from John Arderne's Practica of fistula in ano [see his Pulvis sanguis veneris]. Some of the recipes have encrypted titles, e.g. Bprbczs pulcrvm (f. 3:174r). Several of the recipes in this collection are associated with medical practitioners: Pro Gomorria secundum M W. Castelle (f. 3:172v) Pro Vlceracione Reins faict per Apultrewyk per M. W. Castell (f. 3:173r) Vnguentum Terbentius secundum ffratrem W. Holm (f. 3:177v) Contra [...] Pro Thoma lopham (f. 3:177v) Emplastrum pro Lumbis rembz per R. K. (f. 3:183r) Emplastrum pro Epate secundum W. Holm (f. 3:183v) Pro calculo et pro stranguria per S. Robert ffille Capell secundum M. (f. 3:184v) None of the aforementioned practitioners have been identified, except for frater W. Holm who must be the Franciscan friar William Holme (fl. c. 1380-1415) whose recipes are frequently cited in the Tabula medicine and who compiled two medical works (see Peter Murray Jones The Medicine of the Friars in Medieval England, Health and Healing in the Middle Ages, 5 (Woodbridge: Boydell and Brewer, 2024), pp. 74-96).

work: title: Collection of medical, horticultural, magical, and culinary recipes
bibliography: note(s): The collection includes a medical recipe to treat scabies (Pro Scabie); culinary recipes, including instructions for preserving fruit to serve fresh at Christmas (ffor to kepe Cheries or bolas or plumbes ffresh vnto Christmasse) and to make ale that has gone sour drinkable again (ffor to make ale that is sower to turne into his own kende ayen); horticultural recipes, including instructions for making roses grow throughout the year (Ad custodiendas rosas per totum annum) and to make them grow faster (vt roras cicius habere possis);. a chemical recipe to carry fire by hand without hurting oneself (Ad portandum ignem in manibus tuis sine lesura; magical recipes, including instructions for making a herbal amulet invoking the names of the Archangels against enemies (Vt inimicus fugiet te); for making an amulet with celandine collected in the morning of the feast of St Peter ad Vincula (1 August) in order to enable its user to escape any prison; to secretly open a wax seal (Ad aperiendum ceram) by placing violet roots under an altar for nine days and then blowing its powder onto the seal [this recipe also occurs in the so-called Cambridge Book of Magic; see Paul Foreman (attributed) The Cambridge Book of Magic: A Tudor's Necromancer's Manual, ed. by Francis Young (Cambridge: Texts in Early Modern Magic, 2015), p. 59]; to make an amulet from hart's tongue in order to learn the art of jesting (Ad sciendum qualiter ioculatores faciunt); to make a drink from chamomille to determine whether a woman is a virgin (Ad sciendum an mulier sit virgo vel ne); Ink and pingment recipes:, to soften steel (Ad mollificandum calibem), to harden steel (Ad indurandum calibem), to make coloured gilded or silvered letters Ad colorandum litteras sculptas in metallo quocumque colore and a recipe for catching fish (Ad capdiendum pisces).
bibliography: bibl: Paul Foreman (attributed) The Cambridge Book of Magic: A Tudor's Necromancer's Manual, ed. by Francis Young (Cambridge: Texts in Early Modern Magic, 2015), p. 59; eVK2 4099.00; Mooney (1995), pp. 85-85 [other copies of individual recipes]

work: title: Collection of medical, chemical, magical, and trick recipes
bibliography: note(s): The collection includes recipes to stop someone from sleep-talking (Pro loquentibus in sompnis); whiten teeth (Ad dentes dealbandum); grow hair (Ad faciendum caput habere crines carens crinibus); depilate (Ad tollendum glabram); make it seem that one's house is filled with wild beasts (Vt aliqua domus appareat plena feris); make prunes fall from a tree without touching the tree or fruit (Vt pruna cadant de arbore et non appropiabunt arborem nec fructum manus nec lapis nec lignum); give a black horse a white colour (Ad faciendum nigrum equum . album); carry fire by hand without hurting oneself (Si vis ferre ignem in manibus tuis); make a non-extinguishable candle (Vt candela non extingeatur propter ventum nec per pluviam); make headless persons appear in a house (Vt homines existentes in domo appareant sine capitibus); clear one's voice (Ad vocem clarificandum); turn vinegar into wine (Vt acetum in vinum redeat); turn wine into vinegar (Vt vinum acetum fiat); shoot an arrow or thorn (Ad sagittam vel spinam eiciendum); learn whether or not a disease will kill a patient (Si vitam vel mortem alius aegri inuestigare volueris); turn a red rose into a white one (Ad rosa rubea deueniant alba; pull teeth (Ad depondendum dentes; whiten one's face or hands (Ad faciem vel manus dealbandum); stop a 'harlot' from lusting (Ad faciendum meretricem cessare de luxuria); make someone dream (Ad faciendum ipnkmsn semetipsum tppnkbsf, which can be decrypted as: Ad faciendum hominum semetipsum somniara); make a donkey follow you (Si vis quod as sequitur te); make oneself invisible (Si vis esse invisibilis); and catch birds (Ad aues recoligendum similiter).
The recipes are for treating the pestilence and gall or bladder stones.

work: title: Collection of about 200 medical recipes and charms
paratext: incipit: 100r Here bygynnes a tretyce of oyles and wateres medicynabell and how þei sschal be made and for what malady þei are gode and furst of oyle of rose þat ys made of mony maneres
paratext: explicit: 113r and mell þen þe water þerwyth and boyle hit agayn and lay to þe sore in maner of a plaster and he schal be hooll amen
paratext: rubric(s): 100r In nomine domini Jhesu Amen . quod ix. xiij.
bibliography: note(s): The collection includes various charms: One charm, entitled A good medycyn for the ffeueres (f. 100r) invokes seven types of fevers that are named after their durations, starting with a one-day fever (cotidianas) and going up to a seven-day fever (septanas). Another charm, entitled Another for þeo same (ff. 100r-100v) instructs one to write holy names of God on three oblates and feed them to a patient over the course of three consecutive days. One for curing a morbid growth in the eye, entitled Coniuracyoun for þe hawe in þe ye a souereyn medycyn (f. 101v) involves a formula that needs to be recited over the eye and yellow juice of celandine that needs to be applied with a goose feather (þe fether of a gos wynge þat þis goldesmythe vses to soude with) that needs to be bound over the eye all night for a duration of ten days. There is also a charm for curing toothache, entitled A nobell charm for tothache (f. 102v) that recounts the apocryphal tale of Christ on a marble stone healing St Peter from the tootache. A charm against dysentery, entitled A good charme for þe menysoun (f. 104r), conjures the ailment with the apocryphal story about how the River Jordan stopped flowing at Christ's baptism. Under a heading, entitled A good charme to staunche blode of man or woman (f. 105r six charms for bloodstaunching are given: the first one invokes the apocryphal story of Longinus piercing Christ's side; the second to fifth charms involve liturgical formula and prayers often in combination with herbs; and the sixth charm involves two strips of parchment inscribed with magical characters that need to be bound between the patient's shins (including a test to prove the efficacy of these charaters by writing them on a knife and subsequently cutting a swine with it). It also contains a magical method for determining whether a patient shall live or die, entitled ȝef þy gode frend be seke and þou wylt wyte wheþer he schal lyue oþer dye (ff. 107r), in which one needs to recite five Pater Nosters over five shoots of vervain in honour of the Five Wounds and then conjure the shoots that the patient shall tel them truthly whether they will live or die, place the herb in one's right hand and then hold the patient's right hand with the herb in between the joint hands. The medical practitioner should then ask the patient wheter they will live or die and he schal say þe sothe. A charm, entitled ffor þe ffalyng euell (f. 110r), instructs one to take blood from the patient's little finger and use it to write the names of the Three Magi either on a parchment amulet or, for a child below the age of seven, in a drinking cup. Another charm to help patient's sleep, entitled ffor hym þat not slepe for sykenus wryte þes wordes on a lorere leeff (f. 112r), involves an amulet inscribed with the words: + Ymael + Ysmahet + Adiuro te per angelum dei vt soporet homo iste that needs to be placed secretly under the patient's head. Two childbirth charms, one is an instruction for making an amulet (unspecified material) inscribed with Maria peperit christum formula, including reference to St Celine [Cecilia] and St Remigius, and the formula Sator Arepo Tenet Opera Rotas, that needs to be bound to the pregnant woman's belly. The other involves inscribed the Pater noster in a drinking bowl and making the pregnant woman drink ale or wine from it. A charm for the toothache, entitled A charm for þe totake or for what worme þat be in þe hed or in any place of þe body (f. 113r), an amulet inscribed with a charm that invokes vermin by the Virgin Mary and St Cassian; and a charm to heal fever, entitled ffor þe feuerez a good medycyne (f. 113r) that invokes the names of God. Two recipes are attributed to a certain John Norton: one (f. 113r). was initially attributed to J. Weston but this name has been crossed out and replaced for: 9.13, which has been decrypted to J. Norton to the right. Another recipe on f. 100r has also been attributed to him: Quod ix. xiij.

work: title: Encrypted instruction for harnessing the magical properties of vervain in order to open locked doors
paratext: incipit: 114r R xfrxfnbm bntf xrtx spl kn xkg bssxpcpks bf mbrkf . skccb ft pxlxksb ft ppk pxlxfm kn prf txp ft flb kn sfrbm ft stbtkm bpkft
bibliography: note(s): Attributed to a 'J.C.': .9.3., using the same substitution cipher as found in attributions to John Norton (see f. 115r and Part 4: Provenance).; This text can be decrypted as follows: Recipe ueruenam ante urtum [sic: ortum] solis in assumpcionis beate marie sicca et puluerisa et poni [sic: pone] puluerem in ore tuo et fla in seram et statim aperiet.; The text instructs practitioners to collect vervain before sunrise on the Feast of the Assumption of Mary (15 August), dry and pulverise the herb and its powder into their mouths, and then blow the powder into a lock. This instruction is comparable to an instruction in a collection of necromantic experiments compiled by Paul Foreman in the 1530s (now Cambridge, University Library, MS Add. 3544 the so-called Cambridge Book of Magic). Although the latter instruction, does not involve vervain but the root of violet, it similarly instructs the user to blow powder of the herb on wax in order to secretly open sealed letters: cum ceram aperire vis pone in ore tuo et fla super ceram et stati aperietur (see Paul Foreman, The Cambridge Book of Magic: A Tudor Necromancer's Manual, ed. and trans. by Francis Young (Cambridge: Texts in Early Modern Magic, 2015), p. 59 [no. 28]). Interestingly, this very same magical instruction for opening wax seals can be found among a collection of recipes on ff. 83r-84r in Part 2 of O.2.13.

This copy is not recorded in Catherine Eagleton, Monks, Manuscripts and Sudials: The Navicula in Medieval England, Medieval and Early Modern Philosophy and Science Series, 11 (Brill: Leiden, 2010). Eagleton lists and identifies sixteen manuscript copies of five different texts on the navicula (including copies in Cambridge, Trinity College, MS O.5.26 and Cambridge, Trinity College MS O.8.16). The newly discovered copy belongs to Eagleton's Group A of Navicula manuscripts, which survives in ten manuscripts (including Cambridge, Trinity College, MS O.5.26 and Cambridge, University Library, MS Gg.6.3 [diagrams only]). The newly identified copy opening is comparable to two Group A manuscripts: London, Royal College of Physicians, MS 384 and Oxford, Bodleian Library, MS Wood D.8.

paratext: incipit: 2:61r Seace sorrow now for thow hast don the deed / Lo care hath now consvmd my carcas quit / No hepe can helpe nor helpe can stand insted / ffor dolfull death doth cutt off all delight / Yet whilst I heer the towling of the bell / Before I dye I wright this faint farwell
paratext: rubric(s): 2:61r A faint farwell off a faithfull frend dispairing to live after her frendes departure
bibliography: note(s): Full transcription. Previously unidentified copy of Weelkes' work. The poem is almost identical to that found in Madrigals to Three, Four, Five and Six Voyces (1597) but there are minor variations. For example, the last line appears to have been deliberately changed to adapt the poem to a literary-manuscript context: while the Madrigal version has: before I dye, Ile sing my faint farewell, the version in this manuscript gives: Before I dye I wright this faint farwell.

paratext: incipit: 2:61r ffancy farwell you wroughtst my fond delighte / Delight adue the cawre of my distresse
paratext: explicit: 2:61v ffolly farwele that I have fancyed so / And farwell fancy that first wrought my woe
bibliography: note(s): This appears to be a previously unknown poem by Thomas Weelkes as it is not included in David Brown, Thomas Weelkes: A Biographical and Critical Study (London: Faber and Faber, 1969). Aside from the fact that the poem is attributed to a T.W., this poem fits thematically well with other works by Weelkes, for example his Farewell, my joy (1598). It is possible that this poem is a direct continuation of Cease Sorrows Now, and that both form a single work for the faithfull frend who is mentioned in the title written above the preceding poem.
bibliography: bibl: David Brown, Thomas Weelkes: A Biographical and Critical Study (London: Faber and Faber, 1969)

bibliography: note(s): The collection is described as dedicated to metallic inks in Mooney (1995), p. 161. It indeed opens with such recipes, including one for writing with gold or silver that is said to have been proved by a certain 'faskin' (probat est per faskin). However, the collection actually covers a much wider range, including recipes to make spirit ('aqua ardens'), red wax, and gunpowder; to capture fish with your hands; to make someone fall asleep; to cure the 'stone'; to make yourself invisible by placing the heart of a toad on your foot; to prevent dogs from barking at you; and to stop someone from talking in their sleep. The collection also features a charm for finding stolen goods (Pro furto inueniendo) on f. 77v. The latter requires the victim to place a piece of virgin wax inscribed with the names of the Three Magi, Dismas and Gestas, under their head when they go to sleep. After nine nights they will see the location of their goods in a dream.

work: title: Medical recipes, including excerpts from the Chirurgia of Roger of Salerno and Roland of Salerno
paratext: incipit: 106r Confectio nostri ruptorij que sic fit . Recipe cineres de sarmentorum et cineres stipitum fabarum ana libri iiij et in fundantur in aquam calidissimam
paratext: explicit: 108r inflaciorum tere caules virides et cathaplasma vel ex apozumate fit
bibliography: note(s): In the same hand as the works of Henri de Mondeville on ff. 1r-106v. Text ends abruptly. Headwords in the outer margins describe preparations to treat 'Ruptorium cirurgicorum', how to treat 'carbunculum', how to treat 'apostemata', how to make an 'emplastrum philosoforum', how to make an 'emplastrum album', how to treat 'fistula in ano', how to treat 'squinancia', and how to treat pain in the 'mamillis'. The 'fistula in ano' section begins at the top of f. 107r: 'De fistula in ano . Iuxta fundamentum quandoque nascitur fistula vel apostema', and despite the similarity of the heading in the manuscript to the famous work by John of Arderne, this treatment appears to derive from the Chirurgia of Roger of Salerno compiled by Roland of Salerno. The Chirurgia of Roger and Roland was edited by de Renzi et al., Collectio Salernitana, II:426-496 and the 'fistula in ano' treatment in MS O.8.31 on f. 107r is a close match for the Chirurgia, III:48, printed by de Renzi et al., Collectio Salernitana II:485-486.

language: text lang(s): Latin with occasional plant names glossed in Middle English
bibliography: note(s): Title added in the outer margin of f. 165r in ink in an early modern hand 'Tractatus Medicina in quatuor Libri Distinctus'. ; Various capitulae in this item are taken from the Latin translation of the De materia medica of Dioscorides Dioscorides Pedanius, of Anazarbos . De materia medica was translated from the original Greek into Latin in Late Antiquity and was popular in north western Europe throughout the middle ages, where it was translated into Latin more than once, and also into vernacular languages in the later medieval period. The Latin version of the De materia medica that seems most closely related to parts of the text in MS R.14.31 was edited primarily from Munich, Bayerische Staatsbibliothek, Clm 337 by Hermann Stadler across several articles around the turn of the 20th century. The segments of De materia medica that appear in MS R.14.31 do not appear in the same order that they appear in most typical copies of the Latin text, and it is frequently interpolated with content from elsewhere. Readers may wish to compare the chapter at the opening of 'Book 1' in this item at f. 165v headed 'De edera' and beginning 'Cissos id est edere multe sunt species' with Hermann's edition (p. 244 seq.) and  München, Bayerische Staatsbibliothek, Clm 337, f. 69va (ch. PΞE) and then note the subsequent divergence of Trinity MS R.14.31 from the text in BSB Clm 337 in later chapters; this is just one of several points of similarity and then difference between the two manuscripts.

An untitled recipe (f. 3r) has the name D. Bulleyn written over it, probably referring to the English physician William Bullein (b. c. 1515-1576) who published various medical works between 1558 and 1565. A recipe for the dropsy (f. 4r)is attributed to D. Langten, probably referring to the English physician Christopher Langton (1521-1578), fellow of King's College, Cambridge, and the College of Physicians of London, who published medical works between 1547 and 1552. The recipe may not be taken from his published works, however, since it seems to describe an eye-witness account of a medical treatment performed by Langton on a female patient (Mrs Egles) involving her being placed into a newly-dug pit and then being buried with sand taken from the bowling alley. A recipe for a gall or bladder stone (f. 8v) is attributed to Valentine Rawsworme the stranger surgion (and said to have been given to John Hinde). This probably is the Valentine Russwurin whose medical practices were critised by the London surgeon William Clowes (1543/4-1604) [on Russwurin, see Amanda Coates, 'Stories of Medical Malpractice in Elizabethan England', Synapsis(2022)] (with thanks to Peter Murray Jones for sharing his identification). A recipe for frenesie (f. 4r) is attributed to D. Atlone, who remains unidentified. A recipe for the stone (f. 11r) is attributed to D. Bayl, who remains unidentified. ; All the recipes are directly medical except for a recipe for a wasshing ball (f. 9r), which involves Venetian soap (Sope of Venyse). A recipes for a washing ball can be found in Hugh Plat's Delightes for Ladies (London: 1600), involving castille soap.

bibliography: note(s): The accounts refer to persons situated in (in order of appearance) Lewis (levys), London (london), Nottinghamshire (notynghamschyre), Cardiff (kerdyffe in Walys), Henley-on-Thames (henele uppon temse), and Wycombe (Wycombe). They are typically named with their titles and occupations: pryor, knyȝt, squyer, draper, mercer, grocer, habyrdasscher, brever, talov chavndeler, pevterer, dyer, ffyschemonger, wolpacker, taylour, tavyer. While the aforementioned titles and roles all concern men, the accounts include two women: 1. a silkwoman (sylkwoman) who is only identified by her surname: langeton. There were (at least) three silkwomen with that surname: Jane Langton, a silkwoman and merchant in London, who drew up her will in 1475; and her two daughters-in-law Agnes Langton and Elizabeth Langton. The latter supplied the royal wardrobe with silk in 1503 [on them, see Marian K. Dale, 'The London Silkwomen of the Fifteenth Century', The Economic History Review, 4:3 (1933), 324-335 (pp. 327-328)]. 2. A woman who is (again) only identified by her surname Helmys of Henele uppon temse and who is described as the executrix of John Helmys merchant. She has not been identified. The evidence for the dating of the accounts to 1463-64 comes from three entries: 1. An entry for Thomas Cooke who is identified as knyȝt and aldyrman of london. He must be Sir Thomas Cooke (c. 1410-1478), who was alderman of the City of London from 1456 onwards, knighted in 1465, and Lord Mayor in 1462-63 (for him, see also Cambridge, Trinity College, MS O.3.11 and Cambridge, Trinity College, MS R.14.52). 2. An entry that names John as the prior of Lewis Priory. Given the identification of Sir Thomas Cooke, this prior John cannot be John Burghersh, who was prior from 1409 until 1414, or John Ashdowne who occurs as prior in 1506. He can only be John Danyel, who was prior from 1445 until 1464. 3. The final entry that refers to John Frost, mercer, who drew up his will, which identifies William Dunthorn as his executor, dated to 2 July 1463 (see Kew, The National Archives, PROB 11/5/211).

work: title: A list of names or invocation of angelic or demonic spirits
paratext: incipit: 17v Oberyon Ascaryel Bletthe ssybbylla
bibliography: note(s): Full transcription. A previously unnoticed and untranscribed (?) 15th-century addition. Their names can all be found in early modern necromantic rituals. For example, the so-called Folger Book of Magic (Washington, Folger Shakespeare Library, V.b.26, Part 1 and Part 2), a late 16th-century grimoire, features descriptions and conjurations of the spirits Oberyon (I, pp. 76, 113, 115-116, 185, 190-200); Ascariell [Askariell] (I, pp. 169-170); Byleth (I, pp. 78, 87); and Sibilla (II, p. 228). What is especially interesting is that the Folger Book of Magic, identifies Oberyon [Oberon] as 'kinge of the fayries' who can reveal hidden treasure and how it can be obtained. His name in Cambridge, Trinity College, MS R.14.44 then resonates with the alchemical poem on 15r-17r in which Elchizel, Queen of Fairies, provides instructions on how to make silver and gold. Ultimately, all the spirits listed on f. 17v may have been invoked for obtaining wealth.

Therfor to the first invencioun owght to be multiplied bi .xiiij. and the product therof divide bi .x. and it shal shewe
bibliography: note(s): The treatise contains excerpts from Geoffrey Chaucer's Treatise on the Astrolabe on ff. 2:231v-2:234r. ; Blank spaces throughout the treatise indicate that drawings of the described scientific instruments were originally planned but never executed. ; The title or subheading Makyng of a speer etcaetera was added by a later hand to the outer margin of f. 2:215r. ; The treatise's chapters end with reference to a certain Multon: Quod Multon occurs on ff. 2:215r [with the date 1458], 2:217r, 2:219r, 2:222r. The signatures may refer to the London stationer John Multon (d. 1475). The latter may be the 'Hammond Scribe' [see Origin] but Mooney (1995) thinks this unlikely since his name only occurs in this text and not in any other texts in this or other manuscripts copied by the Hammond Scribe. Instead, Mooney suggests that Multon was the source of this work.

Jelys . tarte prune . wardons and oryngis baken . and marche payne redde wyne claret wyne and whyte wyne treheroun tunc marschall; The names in this account of the Christmas feast seem to correspond to members of Lincoln's Inn described in the Black Books of Lincoln's Inn in the years 1517-1520: 'Bowys' is probably the 'Bowes' who was called to the Bar in 1518 (see Black Book, vol. 1, p. 188) 'R hawkeyns' may be the Richard Hawkyns who with a Henry Parker was awarded in 1520 'the chamber Master Goodman' after Goodman's death (see Black Book, vol. 1, p.193) 'wode' is probably the 'Wode' who was elected a govenor of Lincoln's Inn on All Saints Day 1518 (see Black Book, vol. 1, p. 187) 'treheroun' is almost certainly the 'Treheyron' who was elected Marshall on All Saints Day 1518 (see Black Book, vol. 1, p. 187) ; See Baker and Ringrose for further information.

bibliography: note(s): The collection contains three charms: 1. an abracadabra-type of charm in Latin for protection against evil that is called Sigillum Salamonis (f. 28v). 2. A Latin charm for curing epilepsy (gutta caduca) that involves the Pater Noster and Ave Maria. 3. A charm against Crampe that involves the formula Ananizapta (ff. 28v-29r). One or two users have marked the recipes in different ways: with crosses and with the astronomical symbol for Cancer (♋).

work: title: Account of a soul's seven-day journey after death
paratext: incipit: 35r De exitu anime per septem dies primo quidam die quando exit a corpore tendit ad hierusalem ubi Christus passus pro se
paratext: explicit: 35r septa die ad habitaculum proprium si vixerit male ad pena si bona ad requiem
bibliography: note(s): Added in the second half of the 15th century by a different hand than that of the medical recipes. The text appears to be unique, but probably derives from the Visio Sancti Pauli, which describes a similar seven-day journey of a soul after death: Si quidem quando vadit anima de corpore primo ad orientem, diende ad Iherusalem, deinde ad domum quam edificavit Adam, deinde ad Iordanem, deinde ad templum Salomonis, deinde ad Bethleem Iuda, deinde ad montem Oliveti, deinde ascendit scalam ad superna, ubi conveniunt ei quatuor milia angelorum et archangelorum de tartaris preliantes circa anima hominis. Deinde venit ad Ierusalem celestum in septem diebus et die VII iudicatur in conspectu troni, prout gessit sive bonum sive malum (see Lenka Jiroušková, Die Visio Pauli: Wege und Wandlungen einer orientalischen Apokryphe im lateinischen Mittelalter. Unter Einschluß der alttsechischen und deutschsprachigen Textzeugen, Mittellateinische Studien und Text, XXXIV (Leiden: Brill, 2006), p. 538.
bibliography: bibl: Lenka Jiroušková, Die Visio Pauli: Wege und Wandlungen einer orientalischen Apokryphe im lateinischen Mittelalter. Unter Einschluß der alttsechischen und deutschsprachigen Textzeugen, Mittellateinische Studien und Text, XXXIV (Leiden: Brill, 2006), p. 538

work: title: Two magical cures for staunching blood
paratext: incipit: 250v De naso uel plaga fluentem si carecteras subsequentes scribantur et suspendantur circa collum uel brachium alicuius sanguinentus de naso uel de plaga cito restringetur sanguis
paratext: explicit: 250v quo vero desiccato restringetur sanuis ubicumque fuerit sine de naribus sine de plagis
paratext: rubric(s): 250v Ad Sanguinem restringendum
bibliography: note(s): The text describes two methods for staunching blood: the first one involves a magical amulet with characters whose magical properties can be tested by writing them on the handle of a knife and cutting a pig or piglet with it; the second one (probably designed for healing nosebleeds) involves a hazel rod that has to be cut open in the middle so that the patient's head can go through it. Subsequently, a charm should be read over the patient's head and the rod anointed with their blood. Finally, the rod should be pulled over their head and worn by them like a crown until their blood on the rod has dried up. The latter method is accompanied by a marginal illustration (described in the Decoration section below) to which the text explicitly refers: accipe virgam coruli etatis vnius anni et findatur cum cultello per modum ita quod vtrumque caput virge sanum permaneat ad modum sicut hic depingitur. The second magical method for staunching blood may have been derived from an illustrated copy of John Arderne's Liber receptorum medicinalium which contains the very same charm. For example, see the charms and drawings in Cambridge, Emmanuel College, MS 69 (f. 4r) and Cambridge, Trinity College, MS O.2.49 (f. 1v).

paratext: incipit: 6r: though a wyndewe / had nouȝt a shoo
paratext: explicit: 13r: This tale a non / and seide on þis manere

paratext: incipit: 13r: Whilom there was / as olde stories tellen vs
paratext: explicit: 39r: Thus endeth Palamon / and Emelye / And god saue al / this fair companye
paratext: rubric(s): 13r: Iamque domos patrias scithice post aspera gentis / prelia laurigero et cetera / Heere bigynneth / the knyghtes tale

paratext: incipit: 39r: Whan that the knyght / had thus his tale I told In al the companye / ne was þere ȝong ne old
paratext: explicit: 39v: A vyseth ȝow / and put me ouȝt of blame / And eke / men shuln nat make / ernest of game
paratext: rubric(s): 39r: The prologe of the Millere
bibliography: note(s): DIMEV: I.3155-6 omitted

paratext: incipit: 40r: Whilom there was dwellyng / in Oxenford / A riche gnof / that gestes held to bord
paratext: explicit: 47r: And Nicholas is skalded / in the toute / This tale is don / and god saue al the route
paratext: rubric(s): 40r: Heere bygynneth the Millers tale
bibliography: note(s): DIMEV: I.3721-2 omitted.; 'quod Wytton' in the margin of f. 47r.

paratext: incipit: 47v: Whanne folk han laughen / at þis nyce cas / Of Absoloun / and hende Nicholas
paratext: explicit: 48r: He can wel in myn eye / sen a stalke / But in his owen / he can nat sen a balke
paratext: rubric(s): 47v: ...and bygynneth the prologe of the Reve

paratext: incipit: 48r: At Trompyngtoun / nat fer fro Caumbrygge / There goth a broke / and ouer that a brygge
paratext: explicit: 52v: Saue al this companye / grete and smale / Thus haue I quyt the Millere / in my tale
paratext: rubric(s): 48r: Here bigynneth the Reues Tale
bibliography: note(s): 'quod the Reve' in the margin of f. 52v.

paratext: incipit: 52v: The Cok of Londoun / while the Reve spak / For ioye him þought / he clawed him on the bak
paratext: explicit: 53r: And ther with alle / he lough and made chere / And seide his tale / as ȝe shuln after here
paratext: rubric(s): 52v: ...and bigynneth the prologe of the Cook

paratext: incipit: 53r: A prentys whilom / dwelled in oure Citee / Of a craft / of vetayleres was he
paratext: explicit: 53v: And had a wyf / þat held for countenaunce / A shoppe / and swyued for hire sustenaunce
paratext: rubric(s): 53r: The Cookes Tale
bibliography: note(s): A 13-line gap follows the end of the text, with the rubric on the following recto.

work: title: Introduction to the Man of Law's Tale
paratext: incipit: 54r: Oure host saw wel / þat the bright sonne / The ark of his artificiale day / hath ronne
paratext: explicit: 55r: And with that word / he with a sober chere / Bygan his tale / as ȝe shuln after here
paratext: rubric(s): 54r: ...et Incipit prologue legis periti

paratext: incipit: 55r: O hateful harme / condicione of pouerte / With thrust with cold / with honger so confounded
paratext: explicit: 55v: Ner that a Marchaunt / gon is many a ȝere / Me taught a tale / which þat ȝe shal here
paratext: rubric(s): 55r: ...et incipit fabula eiusdem

paratext: incipit: 55v: In Surrye whilom / dwelled a companye / Of chapmen riche / and ther to sad and trewe
paratext: explicit: 67r: Ioye after woo / gouerne vs / in his grace / And kepe vs alle / that ben in this place
paratext: rubric(s): 55v: incipit fabula dame custanus
bibliography: note(s): Opening rubric added by a later hand.; DIMEV: II.530-710 lost.; 'Amen quod Wytton' in the margin of f. 67r.

paratext: incipit: 67r: Experience / though noon auctoritee / Were in this world / is right I now for me
paratext: explicit: 76v: If I haue lycence / of this worthy Frere / Ȝis dame quod he / tell forth / and I wyl here
paratext: rubric(s): 67r: Incipit prologue vxoris de Bathe
bibliography: note(s): DIMEV: Includes III.44a-f.

paratext: incipit: 76v: In the olde dayes / of kyng Arthour / Of which that Bretons speken / gret honour
paratext: explicit: 81r: And olde and angry / nygardes of despence / God send hem sone / verray pestilence
paratext: rubric(s): 76v: ...et incipit fabula vxoris de Bathe
paratext: final rubric(s): 81r: Hic desinit fabula vxoris de Bathe...

paratext: incipit: 81r: This worthy Lymytour / this noble frere / He made alwey / a maner louryng chere
paratext: explicit: 81v: And after this / he seide vn to the Frere / Telleth forth ȝoure tale / myn owen maister dere
paratext: rubric(s): 81r: ...Et incipit prologus fratris

paratext: incipit: 81v: Whilom there was dwellyng / in my contree / An Archedekene / a man of hey degree
paratext: explicit: 85v: And preyeth that theise Sompnours / hem repent / Of here mysdedis / or that the fend hem hent
paratext: rubric(s): 81v: Incipit fabula fratris

paratext: incipit: 85v: This Sompnour / in hise stiryopes heye stode / Vp on this frere / his hert was so wode
paratext: explicit: 86r: God saue ȝow alle / saue this cursed Frere / My prolog wol I ende / in this manere
paratext: rubric(s): 85v: ...Et incipit prologus Summonitoris

paratext: incipit: 86r: Lordyngges there is / in ȝorkshire as I gesse / A mersshy contre / called holdernesse
paratext: explicit: 92r: And Iankyn hath I wonne / a newe Govne / My Tale is doon / we ben almost at Tovne
bibliography: note(s): DIMEV: III.1963-4 reversed.; 'quod Wytton' in the margin of f. 92r.; A 9-line gap between the final line and the final rubric.

paratext: incipit: 92v: Sire Clerk of Oxenford / oure host sayde / ȝe ride as stille and coy / as dooth a mayde
paratext: explicit: 93r: Saue he wole conueyen / his matere / But this is the tale / which þat ȝe moun heere
paratext: rubric(s): 86r: ...et incipit prologue clerici de Oxonia

paratext: incipit: 93r: There is right at the west side / of Ytaille / Doun at te rote / of vesulus the colde
paratext: explicit: 105v: Be ay of chere as light / as lef on lynde / And late him care / wepe / wrynge / and waille
paratext: rubric(s): 93r: ...et incipit fabula clerici de Oxonia
bibliography: note(s): DIMEV: IV.59-60 reversed

paratext: incipit: 105v: This worthi clerk / whan ended was his tale / Oure host seyde / and swor by godys bones
paratext: explicit: 105v: As to my purpos / wyst ȝe my wylle / But thyng that wol nat be / lat it be stille

paratext: incipit: 106r: Wepyng and waylyng / care and other sorwe / I knowe I now / on Euen and on morwe
paratext: explicit: 106r: Gladly quod he / but of myn owen sore / For sory hert / I telle may nomore
paratext: rubric(s): 105v: ...et incipit prologus of the Marchaunt

paratext: incipit: 106r: Whilom there was dwellyng / in lumbardie / A worthy knyght / that born was of Pauye
paratext: explicit: 119r: Thus endeth heere my tale / of Ianuarie / God blisse vs alle / and oure lady Seynt Marie
bibliography: note(s): DIMEV: IV.1405-6 reversed.; 'Amen' in the margin of f. 119r.

paratext: incipit: 119r: Ey goddis mercy / seide oure hoost tho / Now swich a wyf / I preye god kepe me fro
paratext: explicit: 119v: And eke my wyt / suffiseth nat therto / To tellen al / wherfore my tale is do
paratext: rubric(s): 119r: ...Et incipit prologue Armigeri

paratext: incipit: 119v: Squyere come ner / if it ȝoure wylle be / And seye som what of loue / for certes ȝe
paratext: explicit: 119v: Haue me excused / if I speke amys / My wyl is good / and lo my tale is this

paratext: incipit: 119v: At Sarray / in the lond of Tartarye / There dwelled a kyng / that werred Russye
paratext: explicit: 127r: For Canacee / or that he myght hire wynne . And there I lefte / I wil aȝein begynne
paratext: rubric(s): 119v: ...et Incipit favula Armigeri
paratext: final rubric(s): 127r: Explicit Secunda pars / Here endith the Squyeres tale / as meche as Chaucer made
bibliography: note(s): DIMEV: V.69-72, 671-2 omitted.; Remainder of f. 127r and all of f. 127v left blank (with additions made later to the verso).

paratext: incipit: 129r: She seide sire / sithe of ȝoure gentillesse / ȝe profre me / to haue so large a reyne
paratext: explicit: 138v: Now telleth me / or that ȝe ferthere wende / I can namore / my tale is at an ende
bibliography: note(s): 'Amen' in the margin of f. 138v.; DIMEV: V.709-53, 1472-564 lost; 1455-6 omitted.

paratext: incipit: 138v: There was as telleth / Titus liuius / A knyght / that called was Virginius
paratext: explicit: 141v: Therfore I rede ȝow / this counseil take / Forsaketh synne / er synne ȝow forsake
paratext: rubric(s): 138v: ...and bigynneth the Phisiciens tale / with outer a Prologe

paratext: incipit: 142r: Oure hoost bygan to swere / as he were wood / Harrowe quod he / by nayles and by blood
paratext: explicit: 142r: I graunte I wys quod he / but I must thynke / Vpon som honest thyng / whil that I drynke
paratext: rubric(s): 141v: ...abd bigynneth the prologe of the Pardonere
bibliography: note(s): DIMEV: VI.297-8 omitted.

paratext: incipit: 142v: Lordynges quod he / in chirches whan I preche / I peyne me to haue / an hauteyn speche
paratext: explicit: 143v: Which I am wont to preche / for to wynne / Now holde ȝoure pees / my tale I wol bigynne
paratext: rubric(s): 142r-142v: Radix omnium malorum est Cupiditas ; Ad Thymotheum . 6o | The Pardoners owyn Prologe
bibliography: note(s): DIMEV: VI.333-4, 346 omitted; spurious lines follow 345.

paratext: incipit: 144r: In Flaundres whilom / was a compaignye / Of ȝonge folk / that haunteden folye
paratext: explicit: 149v: And as we diden / lat vs laughe and pleye / Anoon they kisten / and reden forth here weye
paratext: rubric(s): 143v: Et nunc narrat fabulam suam
bibliography: note(s): Remainder of f. 149v and all of f. 150r left blank (with additions made later to both).

paratext: incipit: 150v: A Marchaunt whilom dwelled / at Seynt Denys / That riche was / for which men helde him wys
paratext: explicit: 154v: Me semed so / as by his countenaunce / But nathelees / by god oure heuene kyng
paratext: rubric(s): 150v: Here bigynneth the Shipmans tale / next folwyng the Pardoner
bibliography: note(s): DIMEV: VII.394-434 lost.

paratext: incipit: 156r: Lady thyn bountee / thyn magnificence / Thy vertu / and thyn gret humylitee
paratext: explicit: 156r: Right so fare I / and therfore I ȝow preye / Gydeth my song / that I shal of ȝow seye
bibliography: note(s): DIMEV: VII.443-73 lost.

paratext: incipit: 156r: There was in Assye / in a gret Citee / A monges cristene folk / a Iewerie
paratext: explicit: 157v: And seide / o dere child / I halse the / In vertu / of the holy Trynyte
paratext: rubric(s): 156r: Here bigynneth the Prioresse hire Tale
bibliography: note(s): DIMEV: VII.647-690 lost.

paratext: incipit: 159r: But he was chast and no lechour / And swete as is the brambel flour / That bereth the red hepe
paratext: explicit: 160r: As dede the knyght Sire Percyuelle / So worthy vnder wede ; Til on a day
bibliography: note(s): DIMEV: VII.712-44 lost. The final line (918) follows 917 in the margin, written as if one line, separated only by a punctus elevatus.; Rhyming couplets accompanied by a brace and a third line of verse.

paratext: incipit: 160r: Nomore of this / for goddes dignytee / Quod oure hoost / for thow makest me / So wery / of thyn verray lewednesse
paratext: explicit: 160v: And þerfore herkeneth / what that I shal seye / And lat me tellen al my tale / I preye
paratext: final rubric(s): 160v: Here endeth Chaucers tale of Thopas and the prologe of Melibeus...

paratext: incipit: 160v: A ȝong man called Melibeus myghty and riche / bygat vpon his wyf / that called was Prudence
paratext: explicit: 177r: þat he wole for ȝeuen vs oure giltes / and bryngen vs to the blisse / that neuere hath ende ; Amen
paratext: final rubric(s): 177r: Heere is ended Chaucers tale of Melibe...
bibliography: bibl: IMEP 19, p. 8.; Wells XVI:66; IPMEP 18; Benson and Robinson (1987), pp. 217-239

paratext: incipit: 177r: Whan ended was my tale / of Melibe / And of Prudence / and hire benygnetee
paratext: explicit: 178v: As now it cometh / vn to my remembraunce / Haue me excused / of myn ignoraunce
paratext: rubric(s): 177r: ...and bygynneth the Prologe of the Monks tale

paratext: incipit: 178v: I wole be wayle / in manere of tragedie / The harm of hem / þat stoden in hey degree
paratext: explicit: 187r: That hight Daunt / for he can it al deuyse / Fro poynt to poynt / nat oo word wil he faille
paratext: rubric(s): 178v: ...and bigynneth þe Monkes tale þat is titled de casibus virorum Illustrium ; Chaucer
paratext: final rubric(s): 187r: Here endeth the Monkes Tale / de casibus virorum Illustrium
bibliography: note(s): DIMEV: VII.2375-2462 (the 'Modern Instances') follow 2766; 2380 left blank.

paratext: incipit: 187v: Hoo quod the knyght / good sire nomore of this / That ȝe han seid / is right I now I wys
paratext: explicit: 187v: Thanne spak oure hoost / with rude speche and bolde / And seide / vnto the Nonnes preest / a noon
paratext: rubric(s): 187v: Here bigynneth the Prologe of the Nonnes Prest
bibliography: note(s): DIMEV: VII.2810-20 lost.

paratext: incipit: 189r: What eyleth yow to grone / in this manere / Ȝe ben a verrey slepere / fy for shame
paratext: explicit: 195r: As seith my lord / so make vs alle goode men / An brynge vs to his blisse / Amen
bibliography: note(s): DIMEV: VII.2821-2889 lost; 3163-6 omitted

paratext: incipit: 195r: Sire Nonnes Preest / oure hoost seide a noon / I blissed be thy breche / and euery ston
paratext: explicit: 195v: And after that / he with ful merie chere / Seide vn to a nother / as ȝe shuln heere
paratext: final rubric(s): 195v: Heere endeth the Tale of the Nonnes Preest...
bibliography: note(s): Gap of c. 15 lines between final line and final rubric

work: title: Prologue of the Second Nun's Tale
paratext: incipit: 195v: The ministre / and the Norice vn to vices / Which þat men clepen / in Englissh ydelnesse
paratext: explicit: 197r: And brennyng euere / in Charite ful brighte / Now haue I ȝow declared / what she highte
paratext: rubric(s): 195v: ...and bigynneth the Secund Nonnes Tale of Seynt Cecile / With oute a Prologe

paratext: incipit: 197r: This mayden bright / Cecile / as hire lif seith / Was come of Romayns / and of noble kynde
paratext: explicit: 202r: In which / in to this day / in noble wyse / Men don to Crist / and to his seynt seruyse
paratext: final rubric(s): 202r: Heere endeth the Secund Nonnes tale...
bibliography: note(s): 'Amen' in the margin of f. 202r.

paratext: incipit: 202r: Whan that told was / the lyf of Seynt Cecile / Er we had riden fully / fyue myle
paratext: explicit: 204r: Syn þat my lord is gon / I wyl nat spare / Swich thyng as that I knowe / I wil declare
paratext: rubric(s): 202r: ...and bigynneth the Prologe of the Chanouns Ȝeman
paratext: final rubric(s): 204r: Heere endeth the prologe of the Chanouns Ȝeman...
bibliography: note(s): DIMEV: VIII.711 omitted ('deficit versus' in margin); 564-5 precede 562-3.

paratext: explicit: 205v: And of bodies / mollificacioun / And also / of here induracion
paratext: rubric(s): 204r: ...and bygynneth his tale of Multiplicacion
bibliography: note(s): DIMEV: Everything after VIII.855 lost.

The collection contains a cataplasm that is said to have been devised for King Henry VIII: A Cataplasme or Pultas devised for the kinges Maiestie to mitigate payne and agaynste inflamationes and to resolue hardnes (f. 67r). The very same recipe occurs in London, British Library, Sloane MS 1047, ff. 89v-90r, where it is attributed to Henry VIII himself, who is said to have devised it at Hampton Court. The untitled cataplasm on ff. 67r-67v also features in Sloane MS 1047, ff. 90r-90v (with a slight variation at the end), where it is said to have been devised by Henry VIII at St James's Palace. Another untitled cataplasm on ff. 67v-68r can be found in Sloane MS 1047, f. 91r, where it is said to have been devised by William Butts (c. 1486–1545), one of Henry VIII's physicians.

paratext: incipit: 144r Go to þe graue of a ded man and three tymes call hym on his nam at þe hed of þe graue, and say þou N. N. N. I coniure þe, I require þe, and I charge þe bi þi christendome, þat þou hast taken and receyued at þe font stone, and by þe power and might of þe father and of þe sonne, and of þe hollie ghost, þat þou takest leaue of þe Lord Assaell and Nares and thou askest leave this night to come and tell me trewlie of þe tresure þat lyeth hid in such a place or in what place it is, or in what place it lyeth, how I may best com therby, or by what manner of meanes and wayes. Then take of þe earth of þe graue at þe dead bodyes hed, and knitt it in a lynnen cloth, and put it under þe right eare, and sleape ther uppon, and whersoeuer þou lyest or slepest, þat night he wyll com and tell þou trewlie in wakyng or sleping, so þat þou shalt have a uerie iust knowledge of þi desyre whatsoeuer þou shall aske hyme

bibliography: note(s): This is an elementary course on procedure and pleading, perhaps delivered at Oxford, which is mentioned in the precedents. (Mershfeld may have been an Oxford student: see Provenance).; There are a number of different texts called Curia baronis, and their interrelationship is complex. They contain a mixture of guidance in French, with specimens of oral pleading, entries in Latin, and charges and oaths in English. The present text corresponds with CUL MS Gg.6.44, ff. 30v-65r. It is probably from William Kingsmill William Kingsmill's course at Oxford, for which see Baker and Ringrose (1996), pp. 33-34. bibliography: note(s): Note of a grant by an Elizabeth ?Shrop (Scrope) to a Richard Nevyle of the office of steward of a manor. The grant mentions a place called 'Sonyngton' and the text says that that place is also known as 'Sundon' - this probably refers to the manor of Sundon in Bedfordshire, which is spelled as 'Sonedone' and 'Sonyngdon' in various medieval sources. The manor of Sundon came under the control of the Scrope family after the death of its owner Robert Tiptot in 1372. When Tiptot died in 1372, he left behind three young female children, whose wardship was given to Richard le Scrope, 1st Baron Scrope of Bolton (b. c. 1327, d. 30 May 1403). In 1385 Richard le Scrope's son, Roger le Scrope, married Tiptot's daughter and heir Margaret and so the manor of Sundon passed into the Scrope family through that marriage. Although the precise compilation date of CUL MS Ee.5.22 is unknown, the volume probably dates from the final quarter of the 15th century (c. 1485) and there were two Elizabeth Scropes alive in 1485 who may have been parties to the grant. John Scrope, 5th Baron Scrope of Bolton married Elizabeth St John at an unknown date before 10 December 1471; it is not known when the marriage ended, but Elizabeth must have died before 3 July 1494 (and possibly before 1490) as another marriage is recorded for John Scrope after that date. John Scrope, 5th Baron Scrope of Bolton and Elizabeth St John had a son, Henry Scrope, 6th Baron Scrope of Bolton (b. c. 1468, d. c. 1506) who married Elizabeth Percy, a daughter of Henry Percy, 3rd Earl of Northumberland c. 1480. The 'Richard Nevyle' mentioned in the grant probably cannot be identified with any precision as there were several members of the family with that name alive in the late 15th century. The Scropes had a close relationship with the Neville family in the 15th century and had acted as guardians for each others children and had formed marriage alliances between various branches of their families and so this grant doubtless refers to a transaction between these two intertwined families. Much of the text is unclear due to damage to the leaf.
